title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
directAnswer: Find the longest window you can make all-equal by replacing at most k characters. A window is feasible when (windowLength − countOfMostFrequentChar) ≤ k — that difference is the number of replacements needed. Slide a window: expand right, and when it becomes infeasible, shift left by one. Track the answer as the max window size. O(n) time, O(1) space (26 counts).

remember.pattern: Sliding window; valid when windowLen − maxFreq ≤ k
remember.formula:
count = [0]*26
left = 0
maxFreq = 0
best = 0
for right, c in enumerate(s):
    count[c] += 1
    maxFreq = max(maxFreq, count[c])
    while (right - left + 1) - maxFreq > k:
        count[s[left]] -= 1
        left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best
rules: Replacements needed = `windowLength − maxFreq` (keep the majority char, replace the rest).
Window is valid iff that count ≤ k.
Use an `if` (shift left by one) — the window never needs to shrink more than one step per expansion.
You don't need to decrease `maxFreq` when shrinking; a stale-but-too-high maxFreq never produces a wrong larger answer.
Answer is the largest valid window length seen — the window length itself, not maxFreq.
whenToUse: Longest window that becomes uniform/valid after at most k edits
Validity depends on the window length minus a frequency statistic
You can keep a frequency table and a running max frequency
A 'replace up to k' or 'flip up to k' contiguous-window question
antiSignals: Replacements unlimited → answer is just the whole string length
Need zero repeats instead of all-same → Longest Substring Without Repeating
Counting subsequences, not contiguous windows → DP
remember.takeaway: The trick is the validity test `windowLen − maxFreq ≤ k`: the cost to unify a window is its size minus its most common character. Combined with a never-shrink-more-than-one window, that gives a clean O(n) pass — a template for 'longest window fixable in k edits' problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you derive the validity condition windowLen − maxFreq ≤ k and run an O(n) sliding window, and whether you understand why maxFreq need not be decremented on shrink.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Recomputing maxFreq by scanning the whole count array every step (making it O(26n) or worse), or shrinking the window in a while loop that mishandles maxFreq.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the brute force, derive replacements = windowLen − maxFreq, then explain the subtle point: a stale maxFreq can only keep the window from growing, never produce an invalid-but-larger answer, so we never need to recompute it downward.

problemStatement:
You are given a string `s` and an integer `k`. You can choose any character of the string and change it to any other uppercase English character. You can perform this operation at most `k` times.

Return the length of the **longest substring** containing the **same letter** you can get after performing the above operations.
constraints: s consists of only uppercase English letters
understanding: We want the longest contiguous window that can be turned into a single repeated letter using at most k replacements. Within a window, the cheapest way is to keep its most frequent letter and replace everything else — so the cost is windowLength minus the count of that majority letter.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What can I change a character to?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any uppercase letter. So the target letter for a window is whichever already appears most often there.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is k a hard cap or exactly k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most k — using fewer (or zero) replacements is allowed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Substring or subsequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Substring — contiguous. That's why a sliding window fits.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the alphabet size?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 26 uppercase letters, so the frequency table is constant size and the space is O(1).

examples.explanation: Replace the two A's (or two B's) to make "BBBB" (or "AAAA"); the whole string of length 4 works.
Window "AABA" → replace the one B to get "AAAA" (length 4). Or "ABBA" → one replacement.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: A sliding window driven by windowLen − maxFreq is the default; testing every substring is the quadratic baseline.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Test Every Substring
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor the baseline and to surface the 'replacements = length − maxFreq' formula.
hints: The answer is some substring. Given a substring, how many replacements does it take to make it uniform?
Count each letter's frequency in the substring; the cheapest unification keeps the most frequent letter, so cost = length − maxFreq.
For each start i and end j, compute that cost; if ≤ k, the substring is feasible. Track the longest feasible one.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are O(n²) substrings; maintaining counts incrementally as j extends makes each O(1), so O(n²) time. A fixed 26-slot count array → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
For each start index `i`, extend `j` to the right while maintaining a frequency table of the window `[i..j]`. The cost to make that window uniform is `(j − i + 1) − maxFreqInWindow`. If that cost is ≤ k, the window is feasible; record its length. Restart from the next start.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** It encodes the definition directly and, crucially, forces you to articulate the central fact: the cheapest way to unify a window is to keep its most common letter and replace the rest, so the replacement cost is `length − maxFreq`. That formula is the heart of the optimal solution too.

**Why we don't ship this.** Restarting at every start index re-counts overlapping windows. With `n` up to `10⁵`, that's too slow. The waste is the same as in other window problems — when a window starting at `i` becomes infeasible, almost all of the counting for `i+1` overlaps it. A single sliding window reuses that work.
approaches.insight: The brute force pays off by surfacing the key invariant: replacements needed = windowLength − maxFreq. Once you have that, the only remaining inefficiency is restarting the count at each start — exactly what a sliding window eliminates.

dryRun.intro: For each start, extend and check (length − maxFreq) ≤ k.

python.explanation: Track the window's dominant letter count.

pitfalls: Recreating the count array per start — the quadratic cost.
Computing cost as length − k instead of length − maxFreq.

approaches.name: Sliding Window + Frequency Table (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'one window, valid while windowLen − maxFreq ≤ k, shift left when it isn't'.
hints: Keep one window and a count of letters in it. The window is valid while (length − maxFreq) ≤ k.
Expand right by adding s[right] and updating maxFreq. If the window becomes invalid, move left forward by one (decrementing that letter's count).

Subtle point: you never need to lower maxFreq when shrinking. A too-high maxFreq only makes the window look valid; but the window can't grow past the best it already achieved, so the answer stays correct.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Both `left` and `right` move forward only, each at most n times → O(n) total. The frequency table is a fixed 26 ints → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a window `[left, right]` and a 26-slot frequency table. Extend `right` one character at a time, incrementing its count and refreshing `maxFreq`. After each expansion, if the window is invalid — `(right − left + 1) − maxFreq > k` — slide `left` forward by one, decrementing the departing character. Record the window length as a candidate answer.

**Why the validity test is `windowLen − maxFreq ≤ k`.** To make the whole window one letter, keep the letter that already appears most (`maxFreq` of them) and replace every other character. The number of replacements is therefore `windowLen − maxFreq`. The window is achievable iff that's within budget `k`.

**Why a single `if`, not a `while`, suffices.** We're after the *longest* valid window. Once the window reaches some maximum valid length, any later expansion that breaks validity only needs the window to shift, not shrink — keeping its size constant while sliding rightward. If the new region is better it'll grow again; if not, the window glides at its current width. So shifting `left` by exactly one per invalid expansion is enough, and the window length is monotonically non-decreasing.

**The subtle bit: why we don't decrement `maxFreq` on shrink.** When `left` advances, the true most-frequent count might drop, so `maxFreq` can become stale (too high). That's fine. A stale, too-high `maxFreq` makes `windowLen − maxFreq` *smaller*, i.e. the window looks *more* valid. But because the window length never decreases, a falsely-valid window of the same size can't produce an answer larger than one we already legitimately achieved — it just lets the window slide. The recorded `best` is only ever updated to a length we genuinely reached when `maxFreq` was accurate. So skipping the (expensive) recomputation of `maxFreq` is safe and keeps the pass O(n).

**Why O(n) time and O(1) space.** Each pointer sweeps the string once; the frequency table is constant size.
approaches.insight: Two ideas combine: 'cost to unify = length − maxFreq' gives the validity test, and 'the longest window never needs to shrink, only slide' lets a stale maxFreq stay uncorrected. Recognizing that a never-shrinking window tolerates an over-estimated statistic is the non-obvious move that keeps this linear.

dryRun.intro: count letters; valid while (windowLen − maxFreq) ≤ 1. Shift left by one when invalid.

code.python:
def characterReplacement(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
    count = [0] * 26
    left = 0
    max_freq = 0
    best = 0
    for right in range(len(s)):
        idx = ord(s[right]) - ord('A')
        count[idx] += 1
        max_freq = max(max_freq, count[idx])
        if (right - left + 1) - max_freq > k:
            count[ord(s[left]) - ord('A')] -= 1
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

Replacements needed exceed budget → window invalid.
Slide left by one; the window glides at constant width.
Window length is the answer candidate, never maxFreq.

python.explanation: Running max frequency; not decremented on shrink (and that's safe).
Window needs more than k replacements → shift left.
Remove the leftmost char and advance left once.
Track the longest valid window length.

pitfalls: Recomputing maxFreq by scanning all 26 counts on every shrink — works but unnecessary; the stale value is safe.
Returning maxFreq or maxFreq + k instead of the window length.
Using a while loop to shrink and then mismanaging maxFreq, producing a wrong (too-short) window.

commonMistakes: Treating the cost as length − k instead of length − maxFreq.
Recreating the frequency table for every start index (the quadratic brute force).
Returning maxFreq instead of the longest window length.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong validity formula
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The replacements needed to unify a window is its length minus the most frequent letter's count — not its length minus k.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning maxFreq instead of window length
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The answer is the size of the longest achievable uniform window, which is right − left + 1, not the frequency of the dominant letter.
